questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design dynamic range properties with batched updates and amortized analysis, leveraging a segment-tree style approach for real-time run-length maintenance.

## Key Concepts

- Segment tree storing (length, pref1, suf1, best1)
- Merge to propagate cross-boundary runs
- Amortized batch updates vs per-item cost
- Cache-friendly iterative layout

## Code Example

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, length=0, pref=0, suf=0, best=0):
        self.length = length
        self.pref = pref
        self.suf = suf
        self.best = best

def merge(a, b):
    length = a.length + b.length
    pref = a.length if a.pref == a.length else a.pref
    if a.pref == a.length:
        pref = a.length + b.pref
    suf = b.length if b.suf == b.length else b.suf
    if b.suf == b.length:
        suf = b.length + a.suf
    best = max(a.best, b.best, a.suf + b.pref)
    return Node(length, pref, suf, best)
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend to range flips (set to 0/1) or range updates? 
- How does performance adapt when B approaches n or L is near n?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a simple real-time data structure for sliding-window distinct counting, including correctness, amortized analysis, and memory trade-offs.

## Key Concepts
- Sliding window maintenance
- Hash map counters
- Amortized analysis
- Streaming memory trade-offs

## Code Example
```python
from collections import deque, Counter
class SlidingDistinct:
    def __init__(self, N):
        self.N = N
        self.q = deque()
        self.c = Counter()
    def batch(self, arr):
        for x in arr:
            self.q.append(x)
            self.c[x] += 1
        while len(self.q) > self.N:
            y = self.q.popleft()
            self.c[y] -= 1
            if self.c[y] == 0:
                del self.c[y]
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt to dynamic N?
- What if value domain is large or unbounded; how would you bound memory?

## Key Concepts
- Online statistics with two accumulators
- Welford’s method for variance stability

## Code Example

class OnlineStats { constructor(){ this.n=0; this.mean=0; this.M2=0; } add(x){ this.n++; const delta = x - this.mean; this.mean += delta/this.n; this.M2 += delta*(x - this.mean); } variance(){ return this.n<2?0:this.M2/(this.n-1); } stddev(){ return Math.sqrt(this.variance()); } }

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Dynamic text processing under streaming updates is common in analytics and NLP; suffix automata provide tight amortized bounds for incremental substring counting.

## Key Concepts

- Suffix automaton (SAM) basics and incremental extension
- Amortized analysis: each character adds at most two states
- Distinct substrings count via sum(len[state] - len[link[state]]) for new states
- Alphabet-size impact: use maps vs arrays for transitions

## Code Example

```python
class SAMNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.next = {}
        self.link = -1
        self.len = 0

class SuffixAutomaton:
    def __init__(self):
        self.st = [SAMNode()]
        self.last = 0
        self.total = 0

    def extend(self, c):
        p = self.last
        cur = len(self.st)
        self.st.append(SAMNode())
        self.st[cur].len = self.st[p].len + 1
        while p >= 0 and c not in self.st[p].next:
            self.st[p].next[c] = cur
            p = self.st[p].link
        if p == -1:
            self.st[cur].link = 0
        else:
            q = self.st[p].next[c]
            if self.st[p].len + 1 == self.st[q].len:
                self.st[cur].link = q
            else:
                clone = len(self.st)
                self.st.append(SAMNode())
                self.st[clone].len = self.st[p].len + 1
                self.st[clone].next = self.st[q].next.copy()
                self.st[clone].link = self.st[q].link
                while p >= 0 and self.st[p].next.get(c) == q:
                    self.st[p].next[c] = clone
                    p = self.st[p].link
                self.st[q].link = self.st[cur].link = clone
        self.last = cur
        # update distinct substrings count
        self.total = sum(n.len - self.st[n].link_len for n in range(1, len(self.st)))
```
